pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Make a Title is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has two short levels, about a minute each.

Every game on this site has a title, a menu and a demo that plays by itself. This one is about how they are made. Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages below, which say where each thing is made.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Up and Down climb a ladder. Space jumps. F2 shows your lives, hit points and score.

The pictures at the start of each level go by themselves after a few seconds, or sooner if you press a key. Nothing in this game hurts you. Leave the menu alone for half a minute and the demo plays.

pages.head: Level 1: A Menu Picture
pages.html:
Level 1: A Menu Picture

A level card comes up, then a list of the title scene's slots with the menu picture's slot marked, then two pictures of the same menu. In the first the menu's words are lost in busy stripes and spots. In the second the board is plain and the words can be read. The last picture is TMENU.GIF, the menu template, with the game's own words drawn in its boxes: every letter lands inside one. That is the whole lesson: the game writes its menu words over your picture, so the picture has to leave a plain place for them.

Then you are in a hall with three signs, a thumbnail of the menu picture on the wall and a door. Walk along, read, and take the door.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 1 is made

  • The slots. Open tdemo.gam in the Scenes editor and look at scene 0, the title and menu scene. Its twelve slots are the picture and sound files a title is made of: Title graphic, Title song, Menu graphic, Menu song, the storyline, the instructions, the credits, the three backdrops and the Demo recording.
  • The menu picture. The Menu graphic slot holds menu.gif, a 320 by 200 picture like any other. The game shows it, then draws its own words on top: the game's name, then Play, Read Instructions, Read Storyline, See Credits, See Highest Scores and Quit, from about the middle of the screen going down, a line every 8 pixels. They are drawn in whichever color of your palette is closest to bright blue, so a picture with no blue in it gets some other color.
  • The plain board. menu.gif has a pale board where those words fall. The busy version in the level's pictures is the same picture with stripes drawn under the words, and the words get lost in it. Draw your art around the board, not under it.
  • The templates. The disk has a template for each picture the game writes on: TMENU.GIF (the menu), TSCORES.GIF (the high scores), TLOAD.GIF and TSAVE.GIF (the load and save lists). Each is the whole 320 by 200 screen with a line every 20 pixels (one block) and a tick every 10, and a hatched box wherever the game can write, labeled with its top-left corner (X, Y), its width and height (W, H) and the color the words come in. The menu's boxes: the game's name at X 96, Y 104, W 152, H 8 (up to 19 letters); the six choices at X 80, Y 120, W 144, H 48; the marker at X 70, Y 121, W 6, H 45; and a note at X 40, Y 80, W 248, H 8 that shows only when a page is missing. Open one in the picture editor and draw around the boxes, not in them. TMENUP.GIF, TSCORESP.GIF, TLOADP.GIF and TSAVEP.GIF are the same boxes on one plain color, to paint over. The marker puts back the color of its top-left pixel when it moves, so keep the marker's strip one color; on the save list, keep each name's row dark, because the names are yellow.
  • The title is a list. The Title graphic slot holds title.lst, a list: a short movie first, then title.gif for twelve seconds. A slot that takes a picture takes a list as well.
  • Before the level. The same trick shows the pictures before this level: its Level intro graphic slot holds one.lst, a list of the card, the slots picture and the two menu pictures, each held for a few seconds.

pages.head: Level 2: A Demo That Plays Itself
pages.html:
Level 2: A Demo That Plays Itself

A card, a list of the title scene's slots with Demo recording marked, and a table of the first records inside this game's own demo. Then another hall: a sign on how to record a demo, a sign on when it plays, a meter of the most a demo can hold, and the last sign on what counts toward that. The door ends the game.

To see the demo, go back to the menu with Esc and leave the keyboard alone for half a minute. Lian walks along the first hall by themself, and then the menu comes back.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 2 is made

  • A demo is a list of key changes. demo.rec is a plain list. Each entry is two numbers: how many ticks since the last change, and a key code. A key being pressed is one code, and being let go is the same code plus 128, so Right is 77 and 205. The table in the level's picture is this game's own list.
  • Recording one. There is no Record choice on the menu, because the DOS game records every time: choosing Play saves the keys you press into a file named after the game, TDEMO.REC here, and the next Play writes over it. Its last key is the Esc you press to leave. The title screen never plays that file by itself: it plays the file in the Demo recording slot. In the web editor, open demo.rec and choose Record again, or make a new recording with Record one by playing: you play, and your keys become the recording. The web player does not write TDEMO.REC when you choose Play.
  • Putting it on the title screen. In DOS, rename TDEMO.REC to DEMO.REC (playing again would write over the first name, not this one) and choose it in the title scene's Demo recording slot. If nobody presses a key on the menu for 30 seconds, the game plays it back through the real game, keys and timing exactly as you pressed them.
  • The meter and the signs. They are ordinary signs and a wall picture cut into blocks, like the thumbnail of level 1. There is nothing to touch: the rooms are halls to walk along and read.

pages.head: What it cannot do
pages.html:
What it cannot do

  • A demo holds 1,000 key changes, no more. Every press and every release is one, so a tap on a key costs two, and a demo is about 500 taps at most. The game does not warn you: after the 1,000th change the recorder stops adding, and the rest of what you played is not in the file. (The limit is RECLEN in the original source.)
  • There is one demo. The title scene has one Demo recording slot, so the game has one demo, not a different one for each level.
  • A demo is only keys. It does not save where the hero was or what the monsters did, so it is only as good as the game's own repeatability. Keep a demo short and in a part of the game that plays the same way each time.
  • The menu's words are fixed. You cannot move them, change their size or choose their words from the picture. Only the picture, and the color it makes them, is yours.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each:

  • Open TMENU.GIF in the picture editor and draw a menu around its hatched boxes. Save it as menu.gif, paint the boxes in a plain light color, and see the words land in them.
  • Replace title.gif and leave the movie before it, or take the movie out of title.lst.
  • Record a demo of your own: in the web editor, open demo.rec and choose Record again; in DOS, play from the menu, walk to the end of the first level, press Esc and rename TDEMO.REC to demo.rec. Then leave the menu alone and see it play on the title.
  • Record a very long one, and see where the demo stops.

The home page's Starters tab has more small games like this one.

box.tagline: Make the first thing they see.
box.back: A small explorer in a blue beanie has two short levels about a game's title. In the first the pictures of the title scene come up, with the menu picture the game writes its words on. In the second a demo that plays itself is taken apart, key by key. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and make a title of your own.

blurb: Two short levels about the first thing a player sees. The first shows the title scene's pictures: the slot that holds the menu picture, and why the picture must leave a plain board, because the game writes its menu words on top. The second shows a demo, a list of key presses that plays on the title screen by itself, how to record one, and the most it can hold. Signs say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and make a title of your own.
